family: Services SETA: ICT and business services

programmes.title: Technical Support
programmes.summary: First-line and second-line support of users, devices, software and basic networks.
programmes.purpose: To turn classroom knowledge of hardware, operating systems, networks and customer service into dependable day-to-day support practice. By the end of placement the learner should be able to receive a problem from a real user, diagnose it logically, fix or escalate it correctly, and document it so another technician could follow what was done.

qualifications.title: Further Education and Training Certificate: Information Technology: Technical Support
qualifications.source_text: SAQA ID 78964: Further Education and Training Certificate: Information Technology: Technical Support, NQF 4, 163 credits (legacy qualification that replaced ID 24293).

qualifications.title: Occupational Certificate: Computer Technician
qualifications.source_text: Related current occupational route: Occupational Certificate: Computer Technician, SAQA ID 101408, NQF 5, 282 credits (QCTO).

to_confirm: Which qualification or skills programme your funded learners are actually registered on, and its current registration end dates.
The workplace experience hours and logbook format required by your Skills Development Provider (SDP).
workplace_requirements: A real or realistic IT environment with live users, a ticketing or job-logging system and at least one mentor who can do the work.
Supervised access to user devices, a stock of spares and a safe workbench.
Basic access to directory, email and remote-support tools (with limited, logged permissions).
tools: Directory and email administration console (limited permissions)
Antistatic wrist strap and mat, screwdriver set, cable tester

outcomes.statement: Receive requests by phone, email, walk-in or portal and log each one as a ticket with accurate details.
Categorise by type, impact and urgency, and apply the service level agreement (SLA).
Update ticket status, record each step taken and close only after user confirmation.
Escalate unresolved tickets with symptoms, tests done and user contact details.

evidence.description: Ticket extract showing a spread of ticket types
Mentor observation of a live call or walk-in

outcomes.statement: Set up new workstations: unpack, connect, image or configure, label and record in the asset register.
Diagnose faults in peripherals, power supplies, memory, drives and displays using substitution and diagnostic tools.
Replace parts under supervision using antistatic precautions and correct tools.
Prepare retired equipment for secure data wiping and e-waste handover.

evidence.description: Job cards with fault, action and test result
Photos of completed installations (no user data visible)

outcomes.statement: Install, update and repair operating systems and common business applications.
Troubleshoot slow performance, startup problems, profile corruption, application crashes and licence errors.
Detect and remove malware using approved tools and report suspected incidents to the security lead.
Back up and restore user data with the user's consent.

evidence.description: Resolved tickets covering at least three fault types

outcomes.statement: Connect users to wired and wireless networks, shared drives and printers.
Check IP settings and use basic tools (ping, ipconfig, tracert) to isolate where a connection fails.
Configure email clients, VPN and remote-access settings as per company procedure.
Report suspected network equipment or ISP faults to the responsible team with test results.

evidence.description: Ticket notes showing the diagnostic path
Mentor sign-off on a supervised printer or Wi-Fi setup

outcomes.statement: Create, change and disable accounts only on an authorised request.
Verify the user's identity before resetting a password or changing access.
Support multi-factor authentication enrolment and recovery.
Follow the joiner, mover and leaver checklist.

evidence.description: Authorised request attached to each account change

outcomes.statement: Explain fixes in plain language and confirm the user understands.
Stay calm and professional with frustrated or non-technical users.
Write or update knowledge-base articles and quick user guides for recurring issues.
Hand over clearly at shift end or when escalating.

evidence.description: At least one knowledge article authored and reviewed by the mentor

programmes.title: Systems Support
programmes.summary: Administration and maintenance of servers, user environments, networks and backups.
programmes.purpose: To develop learners who can keep an organisation's IT infrastructure running reliably and securely. The placement shows how installation, configuration, monitoring, backup and incident handling work under real change-control and service-level pressure. .

qualifications.title: National Certificate: Information Technology: Systems Support
qualifications.source_text: SAQA ID 48573: National Certificate: Information Technology: Systems Support, NQF 5 (legacy; SAQA lists it as past its registration end date, so check teach-out arrangements).

qualifications.title: Occupational Certificate: Computer Technician
qualifications.source_text: Related occupational routes include Computer Technician (SAQA ID 101408, NQF 5) and Cloud Administrator (SAQA ID 118699, NQF 4).

qualifications.title: Occupational Certificate: Cloud Administrator
qualifications.source_text: Related occupational routes include Computer Technician (SAQA ID 101408, NQF 5) and Cloud Administrator (SAQA ID 118699, NQF 4).

to_confirm: The current qualification replacing the legacy certificate for your cohort.
The level of administrative access a learner may hold on production systems under your SDP and employer agreement.
workplace_requirements: A production or realistic test environment with servers, directory services, network equipment and monitoring.
A named mentor with administrator-level competence and a documented change-control process.
A safe test or staging area where the learner can practise before touching production.
tools: Directory services and group policy console
Network diagrams, switch and firewall consoles

outcomes.statement: Install and configure server operating systems and core roles (directory, DNS, DHCP, file and print).
Apply patches and updates in line with the maintenance window and change record.
Create and manage virtual machines under supervision.
Monitor disk, memory, processor and service health, and act on thresholds.
Manage users, groups, shared folders and permissions on authorised requests.
Apply group policies and password rules under mentor guidance.
Run periodic access reviews and remove stale accounts.
Support cloud productivity platform administration where used.

Configure switch ports, wireless access points and basic firewall rules under supervision.
Troubleshoot DNS, DHCP and routing issues using standard tools.
Label and tidy patch panels and cabling, and update network diagrams.
Run, monitor and verify scheduled backups, and investigate failures.
Perform test restores at agreed intervals and record results.
Support disaster recovery drills and record lessons learned.
Monitor storage capacity and report trends.

evidence.description: Test restore record signed by mentor

outcomes.statement: Respond to monitoring alerts, triage severity and escalate according to the runbook.
Contribute to root-cause analysis and post-incident reviews.
Raise change requests with impact, rollback plan and approvals.
Keep stakeholders informed during outages.
Maintain anti-malware and endpoint protection, and check coverage.
Apply hardening standards and remove unnecessary services.
Check licence compliance and software inventories.
Follow least-privilege principles and escalate security concerns.
Maintain runbooks, build documents and configuration records.
Update the asset or configuration database after every change.
Write handover notes for shift changes.

programmes.title: Systems Development
programmes.summary: Designing, building, testing and maintaining software as part of a development team.
programmes.purpose: To move the learner from writing exercises to contributing safe, tested, reviewed code to a real product. The placement should expose the full lifecycle: requirements, design, build, test, release and maintenance.

qualifications.title: Occupational Certificate: Software Developer
qualifications.source_text: Occupational Certificate: Software Developer, SAQA ID 118707, NQF 5, 220 credits (listed by training providers; MICT SETA is the originating quality partner).

to_confirm: Whether your learners are registered for the occupational certificate or a legacy systems development qualification.
The technology stack the host employer uses, so the learning plan matches real work.
workplace_requirements: A development team following a recognisable process (agile or similar) with a backlog, version control and code review.
Development, test and production environments with controlled access.
A senior developer mentor who reviews code and gives regular written feedback.
tools: Version control platform (for example Git hosting)

outcomes.statement: Take part in backlog refinement, planning and daily stand-ups.
Read user stories and acceptance criteria, and ask clarifying questions before coding.
Estimate small tasks and report progress honestly.
Write clean, readable code in the team's language and framework, following coding standards.
Apply data structures, object-oriented or functional principles and error handling appropriately.
Design and query relational databases and consume or build simple APIs.
Break larger tasks into small, committable pieces.

evidence.description: Database scripts or API endpoints delivered

outcomes.statement: Write unit tests and run existing automated test suites.
Reproduce, debug and fix defects, with a clear log of cause and resolution.
Perform peer code reviews and respond constructively to reviews.
Log defects with steps to reproduce, expected and actual results.

evidence.description: Test coverage for the learner's code

outcomes.statement: Use branching, commits, pull requests and merge conflict resolution correctly.
Understand and run the continuous integration pipeline and read build failures.
Deploy to development or test environments under supervision.
Manage configuration and environment settings without hard-coding secrets.
Fix defects in existing code and learn to read unfamiliar code.
Shadow the production support rota and read logs to trace issues.
Follow the hotfix and release process.
Write comments, README files and technical notes others can use.
Communicate blockers early and ask for help in good time.
Record time and tasks as the team requires.
Apply basic secure-coding practice: input validation, safe authentication, protecting secrets.
Respect software licences and company policy on AI-assisted code.
Protect personal information in test data (use masked or synthetic data).

evidence.description: Evidence that test data is masked

programmes.title: Business Process Outsourcing and Contact Centre
programmes.summary: Customer contact handling and back-office processing against quality and service targets.
programmes.purpose: To build confidence and consistency in real customer and process work. Workplace exposure shows the pace, emotional demands, compliance rules and performance measures that a classroom cannot fully reproduce.

qualifications.source_text: Services SETA covers contact centre and business services; related occupational qualifications and skills programmes exist for contact centre agents, team leaders and BPO processors.

to_confirm: The exact qualification title, SAQA ID, NQF level and credits your cohort is registered on.
Which channels (voice, email, chat, social) and which sector rules (for example financial services or telecommunications) the host employer operates under.
workplace_requirements: A live or realistic contact centre or BPO operation with real customer interactions or real transactions.
Headsets, telephony or chat platform, CRM and knowledge base access.
A team leader or senior agent mentor, with call monitoring and a quality scorecard in use.
tools: Chat, email and social media tools

outcomes.statement: Greet, verify identity using the approved questions and record consent where required.
Listen actively, diagnose the need and resolve or route correctly.
Use scripts and compliance statements accurately without sounding scripted.
Manage holds, transfers and call wrap-up within target times.

evidence.description: Monitored call scores and recordings reviewed with the mentor

outcomes.statement: Respond to email, web chat and messaging in a clear, courteous and accurate way.
Use approved templates and adapt them to the customer's situation.
Handle more than one chat at a time when the operation requires.
Meet response and resolution times for each channel.

evidence.description: Sample of written interactions with quality scores

outcomes.statement: Use CRM, telephony, knowledge base and workflow tools correctly.
Capture complete, accurate notes and select the right call reason or disposition.
Update customer records only with verified information.
Understand and track own measures: average handling time, first-contact resolution, quality score, schedule adherence and customer satisfaction.
Take part in call calibrations and coaching sessions and act on feedback.
Set and review a personal improvement plan with the team leader.

evidence.description: Coaching records signed by learner and mentor

outcomes.statement: Process transactions, applications, claims, orders or data capture according to the standard operating procedure.
Check work for accuracy and complete within the turnaround time.
Deal with exceptions and escalate unusual cases.
Complete reconciliations and daily control checks where required.
De-escalate angry or upset customers while staying within policy.
Recognise vulnerable customers, suspected fraud and abusive behaviour, and follow the escalation protocol.
Apply consumer-protection and privacy rules relevant to the sector.

evidence.description: Mentor observation of a complaint call

outcomes.statement: Follow shifts, breaks and workforce management schedules.
Take part in team huddles and share useful customer insights.
Use support services and manage stress and fatigue.

programmes.title: Robotics
programmes.summary: Assembling, programming, maintaining and safely operating robotic and automated systems.
programmes.purpose: To give the learner supervised exposure to real automation: working safely around moving equipment, assembling and wiring systems, programming and commissioning, and diagnosing faults across mechanical, electrical and software layers.

qualifications.source_text: Robotics is delivered through 4IR-related skills programmes and occupational or mechatronics-related qualifications.

to_confirm: The qualification or skills programme, its NQF level and the workplace-hours requirement.
The specific robot platforms, controllers and programming languages the host workplace uses.
workplace_requirements: A workplace with robots, automated cells, or an equivalent training cell with safety systems in place.
A competent mentor (for example an automation technician or engineer) and a written safe system of work.
Safety equipment, lock-out facilities and controlled access to robot work areas.
tools: Robot or training cell with teach pendant or programming interface
Hand tools, torque tools and electrical test instruments

outcomes.statement: Apply lock-out, tag-out and emergency stop procedures every time.
Respect guarding, safe zones and permit-to-work rules.
Contribute to risk assessments and read safe operating procedures.
Use required protective equipment.
Read drawings and schematics and assemble frames, mounts, grippers and end effectors.
Wire power and control circuits and tidy cable routing.
Torque fasteners and check alignment to specification.
Test continuity, polarity and power supply levels before energising.

evidence.description: Photos of completed wiring (before panel closure)

outcomes.statement: Install and calibrate sensors, motors, servos and drives.
Connect to controllers (microcontrollers or programmable logic controllers) and test inputs and outputs.
Interpret datasheets and wiring diagrams.
Write or modify robot programs in the platform's language and teach positions.
Test programs in simulation or at reduced speed before full operation.
Document parameters, versions and changes.
Take part in commissioning and acceptance tests.
Carry out scheduled inspections, lubrication and cleaning from the maintenance plan.
Diagnose faults using multimeters and other instruments, and by reading error codes.
Replace worn or failed parts and verify correct operation.
Keep a fault and repair log.
Monitor running cells and report abnormal behaviour.
Assist with integration with conveyors, vision systems or other equipment.
Support operators with start-up, shut-down and changeover.
Complete job cards, test sheets and handover notes.
Report near misses and defects promptly.

programmes.title: Data Analytics
programmes.summary: Collecting, cleaning, analysing and presenting data so that people can make better decisions.
programmes.purpose: To show that data analytics is a business activity, not only a technical one. The learner should practise turning a vague question into a clean dataset, a defensible analysis and a clear message for decision makers.

qualifications.source_text: Data analytics is offered through 4IR-related skills programmes and occupational qualifications in the ICT field.

to_confirm: The qualification or skills programme, its NQF level, credits and workplace-hours requirement.
The tools the host workplace uses (spreadsheets, SQL, a business intelligence platform, or a scripting language).
workplace_requirements: Access to real or properly anonymised business data with a clear business question.
Access to the tools the team uses, with permissions set by the data owner.
A mentor (analyst or manager) who can explain the business context and review the learner's work.
tools: Scripting environment where the team uses one
Shared drive or repository with version history

outcomes.statement: Clarify the business question with the requester and write it down.
Identify data sources, owners and refresh frequency.
Extract data using queries, exports or connectors as permitted.
Build or update a data dictionary describing each field.
Detect and treat missing values, duplicates, inconsistent formats and outliers.
Join and reshape data from more than one source.
Validate results against totals or known figures.
Document every transformation so it can be repeated.
Calculate key performance indicators and descriptive statistics.
Look for trends, patterns, segments and relationships.
Test assumptions and note limitations of the data.
Ask a peer or the mentor to review the logic.

evidence.description: Analysis workbook, notebook or query set

outcomes.statement: Choose the right chart or table for the message.
Build and refresh dashboards or reports in the team's tool.
Add titles, labels, units and short narrative so non-technical readers can follow.
Check accessibility, for example colour contrast and clear labelling.
Present findings and recommendations in plain language.
Handle questions, admit limits and offer next steps.
Agree deadlines and manage requests professionally.
Apply POPIA principles: use only the data needed, anonymise where possible and control access.
Store files in approved locations and keep version history.
Report data quality problems back to the data owner.
Automate repeated steps through scheduled refreshes, templates or simple scripts.
Suggest improvements to reports and data collection.

programmes.title: Cellphone Repair
programmes.summary: Diagnosing and repairing mobile devices, serving customers and running a small repair workshop.
programmes.purpose: To build speed, accuracy and customer trust on real devices. The workplace shows how diagnosis, parts quality, customer communication and honest pricing fit together in a repair business.

qualifications.source_text: Delivered mainly as short skills programmes (recent funded programmes run from about one to three months), so the exact registration status and credits must be confirmed.

to_confirm: The skills programme or qualification, its credit value and any workplace component.
Whether the programme covers board-level repair or only module replacement and software services.
Applicable consumer, second-hand goods and e-waste rules for the business model.
workplace_requirements: A working repair workshop, retail service desk or equipped repair container with a competent technician as mentor.
Real customer devices, spare parts supply and a clean antistatic workbench.
Ventilation, fire safety and safe battery handling facilities.
tools: Precision screwdriver set, spudgers, suction cups and heat tools
Multimeter and power supply or USB power meter
Soldering station, hot air station and microscope (where covered)
Job card system and parts inventory

outcomes.statement: Receive the device, record make, model and serial or IMEI, and check condition with the customer.
Take photos of existing damage, and confirm what the customer wants repaired.
Explain data-loss risk, ask for consent and agree on the quote, timeframe and warranty.
Complete the job card and issue a receipt or acknowledgment.

evidence.description: Mentor observation of a customer intake

outcomes.statement: Run structured tests: power, charging, display, touch, audio, camera, network and sensors.
Use a multimeter or USB power meter to check current draw and battery condition.
Check for liquid damage indicators and previous repairs.
Record findings and recommend repair, replace or decline.

evidence.description: Diagnostic checklist for at least several devices

outcomes.statement: Open devices safely using heat, suction and picks, and disconnect the battery first.
Replace screens, batteries, charging ports, buttons, speakers and cameras.
Handle adhesives, seals and connectors correctly and reassemble with the right screws.
Reseal or apply replacement seals where the design requires it.
Practise soldering through-hole and basic surface-mount joints under supervision.
Clean boards after liquid damage using approved methods.

Update, reinstall or restore the operating system and apps with the customer's consent.
Back up and restore data, and confirm with the customer afterwards.

Check IMEI status and refuse suspected stolen or blacklisted devices.
Run a final test checklist covering all functions.
Clean the device, return all accessories and show the customer the working repair.
Explain the warranty clearly and record payment.
Follow up on returns and complaints.
Order and track parts and tell customers whether parts are original or aftermarket.
Keep workspace and tools organised and calibrated.
Dispose of damaged batteries and electronic waste responsibly.
Record income, expenses and stock for the repair business.

programmes.title: Laptop and PC Repair
programmes.summary: Diagnosing, repairing, upgrading and building computers, and recovering user data safely.
programmes.purpose: To develop reliable bench skills on real machines. The learner should repair efficiently, communicate honestly with customers, and protect customer data throughout.

qualifications.title: Occupational Certificate: Computer Technician
qualifications.source_text: Occupational Certificate: Computer Technician, SAQA ID 101408, NQF 5, 282 credits (QCTO), which lists PC repair technician among its occupations.

to_confirm: Whether the learner is on the full occupational certificate or a shorter repair-focused programme.
The workplace hours and logbook structure set by the SDP.
workplace_requirements: A workshop with antistatic workbenches, test equipment and a supply of spare parts and test components.

tools: Precision tool kits and test components
Multimeter, PSU tester and cable testers

Back up data before any repair when the customer consents.
Check power-on behaviour, beep or LED codes, BIOS or UEFI settings and storage health.
Run component stress tests and interpret results.
Replace memory, storage drives, batteries, keyboards, fans, screens and power connectors.

Follow antistatic procedures throughout.

Remove malware and repair corrupted installations.

Make sure software licences are valid and recorded.

Set up basic home or small-office connectivity.
Specify and assemble a desktop from components, checking compatibility.

Advise customers on sensible upgrades within budget.

Work within turnaround targets and update the customer on delays.
Run final quality checks and explain the warranty.
Dispose of e-waste and drives correctly and securely.

programmes.title: Drone Piloting and Repairs
programmes.summary: Safe, lawful remotely piloted aircraft operations, data capture, maintenance and repair.
programmes.purpose: To give the learner supervised real-world flight and maintenance experience, which cannot be replaced by simulation where regulation or competence standards require actual flying hours. It also shows how planning, compliance and data handling make flying commercially useful.

qualifications.title: National Occupational Certificate: Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems (RPAS) Pilot
qualifications.source_text: SAQA ID 121161: National Occupational Certificate: Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems (RPAS) Pilot.
SAQA ID 121155: a related qualification whose outcomes include diagnosing and repairing faults in RPAS (confirm exact title and level).

qualifications.title: MICT SETA 4IR Skills Programme: Drone Piloting
qualifications.source_text: MICT SETA 4IR Skills Programme: Drone Piloting (short programme; placement rules vary).

Whether the learner is on a pilot pathway, a maintenance pathway, or both.
Insurance, landowner permission and airspace approvals for each site.

product developer in a small enterprise

reference_pages.title: The framework: SAQA, QCTO and Services SETA
reference_pages.markdown:
| Body or person | Role in workplace learning |
|---|---|
| SAQA | Oversees the NQF and maintains the register of qualifications. Each registered qualification has a record showing purpose, outcomes, credits, level and assessment criteria. |
| QCTO | Quality council for trades and occupations. Registers occupational qualifications and sets the requirements for training, workplace experience and external assessment. |
| Services SETA | The SETA for the services sector. Funds and supports learning programmes, approves workplaces and learner agreements, and performs quality assurance functions delegated by the QCTO. |
| Skills Development Provider (SDP) | The accredited institution that delivers the knowledge and practical skill modules, supports learners in the workplace, and submits evidence for assessment. |
| Employer or host workplace | Provides the real work environment, resources and a mentor, and meets the obligations in the learner or placement agreement. |
| Workplace mentor | The person who guides, supervises and verifies the learner's workplace performance day to day. |
| Assessor and moderator | Assessors judge evidence against the criteria. Moderators check that assessment is consistent and fair. In occupational qualifications a final external assessment is typically conducted at an accredited assessment centre. |

## How occupational qualifications are structured

QCTO occupational qualifications are generally built from three kinds of learning component, followed by an external assessment. Always confirm the exact structure, credits and hours in the curriculum document of the learner's qualification.

| Component | Where it happens | What it covers and how it is evidenced |
|---|---|---|
| Knowledge modules | SDP classroom, online or blended | The theory behind the occupation. Evidenced by tests and assignments set and marked by the SDP. |
| Practical skill modules | SDP workshop, simulated environment or workplace | Hands-on tasks done to a standard. Evidenced by observed performance, work products and practical assessments. |
| Work experience modules | Real workplace | Supervised workplace duties over a set number of hours or tasks. Evidenced by a logbook signed by the mentor, workplace reports and supervisor confirmation. |
| External integrated summative assessment | Accredited assessment centre | A final assessment of the occupation as a whole, usually combining knowledge and practical components. |

Older qualifications built on unit standards use specific outcomes and assessment criteria, often with a portfolio of evidence. The workplace expectations are similar: the learner must show, not just describe, what they can do.

## Workplace readiness checklist

Before a learner starts, the employer, SDP and mentor should be able to answer yes to each point. Check your SDP and SETA documentation for any additional requirements.

- [ ] The employer has a signed placement or learner agreement and understands its obligations.
- [ ] The workplace can offer the duties listed in the learner's profile in Part 5, or has agreed an arrangement for missing duties (for example short rotation or supervised simulation).
- [ ] A named mentor with current competence in the occupation, and time to supervise, has been appointed.
- [ ] The mentor has received the logbook, evidence requirements and contact details for the SDP.
- [ ] Health and safety induction, personal protective equipment and emergency procedures are in place.
- [ ] Access to systems, tools and equipment has been approved with the right permissions and confidentiality agreements.
- [ ] A workplace policy exists on harassment, grievances and reporting concerns, and the learner has been told how to use it.

## Principles of competence assessment

Workplace sign-off is a form of assessment. Mentors should understand the principles assessors apply when they review evidence.

| Principle | In practice |
|---|---|
| Valid | The evidence matches the task the outcome describes. A signed statement that the learner "was present" is not evidence of performance. |
| Authentic | The work is the learner's own. Mentors should be able to say they saw it done or can verify who did it. |
| Current | The evidence is recent and relevant to current tools and practice. |
| Sufficient | Enough evidence across enough occasions to show the learner can do the task consistently, not once. |
| Reliable and fair | Different assessors would reach the same conclusion. Learners are assessed against the same standard regardless of background, and know the criteria beforehand. |
| Competent or not yet competent | Judgement is binary at the point of assessment. "Not yet competent" means more practice and re-assessment, not failure. |

reference_pages.title: The workplace mentor's guide
reference_pages.markdown:
## What a mentor is expected to do

- Welcome and orient the learner, and explain how the workplace runs, who does what and where to get help.
- Plan and sequence duties so the learner is exposed to each duty area in the profile, building from observation to independence.
- Supervise the work, ensure safety and protect the employer's customers, data and equipment.
- Give regular, specific feedback in writing as well as in conversation.
- Verify and sign the logbook only for work that you have seen, or can reliably confirm.
- Communicate with the SDP about progress, problems and any gaps in available duties.
- Model professional behaviour: punctuality, respect, honesty, safety and ethical use of information.

## The first two weeks: an induction checklist

- [ ] Health and safety induction completed and recorded.
- [ ] Workplace rules, code of conduct, confidentiality and POPIA briefing completed.
- [ ] Introduced to the team, key contacts and escalation routes.
- [ ] Access to systems and equipment issued at the correct, limited permission level.
- [ ] Logbook explained; first week's tasks agreed in writing.
- [ ] Expectations on working hours, attendance, dress, communication and reporting absences explained.
- [ ] Learner told who to speak to about a concern, including someone other than the mentor.

| Phase | Typical timing | Learner activity | Mentor role |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Observe and assist | First weeks | Shadows the mentor and team, completes safe low-risk tasks (level O and A). | Explains what is being done and why; checks understanding; corrects early habits. |
| 2. Supervised practice | Middle of the placement | Performs whole tasks with the mentor present or checking afterwards (level S). | Observes, gives feedback, increases complexity, records evidence. |
| 3. Independent performance | Final stage | Performs routine tasks alone and consistently, escalating when appropriate (level I). | Samples work, confirms consistency, completes sign-off. |

## Logbook and evidence

| Good practice | Poor practice |
|---|---|
| Entries made the same day or week, with specific tasks and outcomes. | Entries filled in at the end of the placement from memory. |
| The mentor signs only work they observed or can verify. | Blanket signing of a month's entries without checking. |
| Evidence is attached or referenced (ticket numbers, job cards, photographs, reports) with sensitive information removed. | Vague entries such as "helped customers" or "did repairs". |
| Entries cover all duty areas, including the less exciting ones such as documentation and safety. | Only the favourite or easiest duties are recorded. |
| Feedback and corrective action are recorded, and the learner can show improvement. | No record of mistakes, feedback or learning. |
